question: Released in 1983, Cinematronics's arcade laserdisc game Dragon's Lair was animated by Don Bluth's team and showed full hand-drawn animation on a CRT — revolutionary for the era. The game was simultaneously a sensation and a financial mess for arcade operators. What was the core problem?

question: In 1984's Ghostbusters, the team confronts a giant marshmallow monster in the climactic battle. The Stay-Puft Marshmallow Man was an entirely practical-effect creation directed by which Hollywood special-effects veteran whose other 1980s work included E.T. and Poltergeist?

question: In 1985's Back to the Future, Marty McFly arrives in 1955 wearing his red puffer life-preserver vest. The locals mistake it for what kind of garment, calling Marty 'Calvin Klein' because his underwear says so?
answer: A life preserver (they think he's a sailor who fell off a boat)

A fireman's life vest from the local volunteer station
A Russian air-force flight survival vest from the Eisenhower era

question: In 1985's The Goonies, the film's iconic 'truffle shuffle' scene features Chunk (Jeff Cohen) lifting his shirt and shaking his belly to gain entry to Mikey's house. Cohen was famously typecast by the role. He grew up to be a successful Hollywood professional in what field — not acting?

Restaurant ownership (he opened a Beverly Hills steakhouse)
Real-estate development (he built a luxury hotel chain)

He stopped acting in his teens, calling the experience formative but unsustainable. He maintains friendly relationships with co-stars Sean Astin and Corey Feldman.

question: Released in 1982, John Milius's Conan the Barbarian opens with Conan's father teaching him the riddle of steel before being killed by Thulsa Doom. The opening text-on-screen quote is famously attributed to Nietzsche but actually from a different source. What's the quote and source?
answer: 'That which does not kill us makes us stronger' — Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols 1888
choices: 'That which does not kill us makes us stronger' — Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols 1888
'In steel a man's soul finds its purest test' — fictional, written by John Milius himself
'The sword is mightier than the kingdom' — from Robert E. Howard's Conan stories
'Crom counts the slain, not the conquests' — from L. Sprague de Camp's pastiches
context: The Nietzsche quote is genuine — from Twilight of the Idols (1888), aphorism 8 of Maxims and Arrows. Milius was a self-confessed Nietzschean. The riddle of steel — 'what is steel compared to the hand that wields it' — is Milius's own invention for the film, not from Howard.

question: In 1983's Return of the Jedi, the planet Endor's forest moon sequences were filmed in a real Northern California redwood grove. The Ewoks were performed by little-person actors including Kenny Baker (R2-D2) and Warwick Davis. Warwick was how old when he played Wicket the Ewok?
answer: Eleven years old
context: Davis later starred in Willow (1988), Leprechaun (1993), and Harry Potter (as Professor Flitwick + Griphook the goblin). He was originally cast as a different Ewok and only got the Wicket role when Kenny Baker fell ill. His daughter Annabelle has the same condition (spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita).

question: In 1987's The Princess Bride, the duel between Westley and Inigo Montoya features Cary Elwes and Mandy Patinkin doing most of their own swordplay after weeks of training under Bob Anderson, the same fencing choreographer who worked with what other famous film franchise?
answer: Star Wars (he was Darth Vader's swordsman in the OT)

context: Anderson was an Olympic fencer (1952 GBR) who became Hollywood's go-to sword choreographer. He wore the Darth Vader costume in the lightsaber duels of Empire and Jedi (with David Prowse acting elsewhere and James Earl Jones voicing). He also choreographed the 1973 Three Musketeers.

question: In 1985's Don Bluth animated film The Black Cauldron — actually a Disney production where Bluth's protégé Joe Hale produced — what was the first Disney animated feature to receive a PG rating?
answer: The Black Cauldron itself, in 1985
choices: The Hunchback of Notre Dame, in 1996
context: The Black Cauldron was Disney's most-expensive animated feature at the time ($44M) and bombed. The Horned King's army of cauldron-born undead earned the PG. Don Bluth was NOT involved despite often being credited — he had defected six years earlier.

question: In 1988's Land Before Time, Don Bluth's family-classic animated film was produced by Steven Spielberg and George Lucas's companies. The studio worked with Amblin Entertainment on what other Bluth film also released the same era?

Spielberg never produced Anastasia (Fox Animation) or All Dogs (Goldcrest Films) — those were post-Spielberg Bluth projects. Land Before Time was meant to be a quiet meditative film; the eventual 14 direct-to-video sequels were not Bluth's work.

question: In 1993's Tombstone, the climactic gunfight at the O.K. Corral is historically inaccurate — the real 1881 gunfight lasted approximately 30 seconds and was actually in a narrow vacant lot near, but not in, the O.K. Corral. The real fight killed three of the Cowboys faction. Who was NOT among the dead?
answer: Ike Clanton (he fled the fight unarmed)
choices: Ike Clanton (he fled the fight unarmed)
Tom McLaury (shot by Doc Holliday's shotgun)
context: Ike Clanton had instigated the fight by drunkenly threatening the Earps the night before but ran when shooting started. Tom McLaury, Frank McLaury, and Billy Clanton were killed. Virgil and Morgan Earp were wounded. Wyatt was untouched. Doc Holliday took a graze. The real fight is now reenacted in Tombstone, Arizona for tourists.

question: In Edgar Wright's 2010 Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, the climactic battle with Gideon Graves uses a 'Power of Love' sword Scott earns from defeating Todd Ingram, the third evil ex. What special-ability tag does the Power of Love sword have in the game's UI text on screen?
answer: +2 Against Evil Ex-Boyfriends
context: The sword appears with a Final Fantasy-style item-acquisition screen showing the stats. Scott also earns a Power of Self-Respect sword when fighting his Nega-Scott self. Both swords appear in the climactic Chaos Theatre battle against Gideon Graves.

question: In Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels, Scott's third evil ex Todd Ingram has vegan powers. When he violates his vegan diet, the Vegan Police arrive to strip him of his abilities. What two specific items does Todd eat to trigger the Vegan Police visit in the film?
answer: Half-and-half in his coffee, then chicken parmigiana

question: In Edgar Wright's Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, the band Sex Bob-omb performs throughout the film. The film's music was overseen by Nigel Godrich (Radiohead's producer), with original songs written by which musician known for his 1990s solo career and his work in the band Beck?
answer: Beck (Beck Hansen)
choices: Jack White of The White Stripes
context: Beck wrote 'Garbage Truck' and 'We Are Sex Bob-omb' for the film. Broken Social Scene's Brendan Canning and Kevin Drew also contributed. The Clash at Demonhead's songs (Envy Adams's band) were written by Metric's Emily Haines.

question: The 2023 Super Mario Bros. Movie features Donkey Kong (Seth Rogen) and references the original 1981 arcade game. Cranky Kong (Fred Armisen), Donkey Kong's father in the film, was originally what character in the arcade games?
answer: The original Donkey Kong from the 1981 arcade game

King Kong from a separate Universal Studios franchise
Diddy Kong's grandfather from the SNES Donkey Kong Country games
An entirely new character invented for Donkey Kong 64

question: Released in 1988 and directed by Don Bluth, The Land Before Time depicts a young Apatosaurus named Littlefoot whose mother dies early in the film. The death scene was so traumatic to test audiences that ten minutes of footage was cut to lower the PG rating. Who voiced Littlefoot?
answer: Gabriel Damon, a 12-year-old child actor

Macaulay Culkin, before his Home Alone breakout

question: In 1989's Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, the Holy Grail is hidden in the temple of the Sun in Petra, Jordan. The 'cup of a carpenter' test at the end has Indy choosing between dozens of grails. What's the actual line the Grail Knight delivers when Donovan (Julian Glover) drinks from the wrong one?
answer: He chose poorly
choices: He picked the cup of pride
context: Robert Eddison played the immortal Grail Knight. The drinking-from-the-wrong-cup effect (Donovan rapidly ages and disintegrates) was Industrial Light & Magic's most-complex prosthetic-and-puppet sequence to that point. The line is a near-perfect mirror of 'he chose wisely' moments later.

question: Released in 1984, The Karate Kid was directed by John G. Avildsen, who had won the Best Director Oscar eight years earlier for what other underdog-sport film?
answer: Rocky (1976)
context: Rocky won Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Film Editing in 1977. Karate Kid's emotional structure mirrors Rocky's — the unlikely mentor, the romantic subplot, the climactic tournament. Pat Morita's performance as Mr. Miyagi earned a Best Supporting Actor nomination.

question: In 1987's Predator, the Yautja (the Predator species name was introduced years later) is famously thermal-vision-sighted. The infrared effect on screen was created using a then-cutting-edge technology. What was it?
answer: A real Inframetrics 525 thermal imaging camera, normally used for industrial inspection

Stop-motion overlays composited frame-by-frame in post-production
False-color time-lapse photography exposed through dichroic filters
A custom video feedback loop with chromatic separation lenses
context: The Inframetrics 525 cost approximately $80,000 in 1986. The Predator's thermal POV had to be filmed separately and then matted in. The technology had previously been used to identify roof leaks and electrical equipment failures.

question: In 1990's Total Recall, Paul Verhoeven directed Arnold Schwarzenegger's Mars-spy story. The film's special effects won the Oscar but the production was famously troubled. The Schwarzenegger character is named Doug Quaid (or possibly Hauser, depending on the film's interpretation). What was the original director attached to the project years before Verhoeven took over?
answer: David Cronenberg, who left over creative differences with the producers

context: Cronenberg's vision was reportedly much closer to Philip K. Dick's original short story — psychological-horror-focused rather than action-blockbuster. He left in 1985. The project then went through many directors before Carolco Pictures hired Verhoeven post-RoboCop.

question: In 1986's Aliens, James Cameron's sequel to Ridley Scott's Alien, Ellen Ripley awakens 57 years after the original film. She joins Colonial Marines investigating the colony on LV-426. What's the name of the orphaned girl Ripley rescues from the colony?
answer: Newt (real name Rebecca Jorden)
context: Carrie Henn played Newt; this was her only film role. Newt's family had named her Rebecca but her brother called her Newt because she could 'fit into all the small places.' In Alien 3 (1992), Newt dies in the opening sequence — a creative decision that infuriated Cameron, who had final-cut authority on Aliens but not Alien 3.

question: James Cameron's 1984 The Terminator nearly hired Arnold Schwarzenegger to play protagonist Kyle Reese instead of the cyborg. Cameron met with Schwarzenegger and changed his mind during their lunch. What was the dish that supposedly cinched the casting reversal?
answer: There was no specific dish; Cameron just realized Arnold's bulk and accent fit the Terminator better

Arnold's hostess insisted on Italian, which Cameron found revealingly mild
The lunch was at Schatzi's, Arnold's Austrian-themed Santa Monica restaurant
context: The screenplay had originally Arnold as Reese (the human soldier sent back to protect Sarah Connor). Cameron later said Arnold's physical presence and the Austrian accent made him ideal for the unstoppable cyborg. Lance Henriksen had been considered for the T-800 and got the role of Detective Vukovich instead.

question: Andre the Giant played the friendly giant Fezzik in 1987's The Princess Bride. The 7-foot-4 wrestler was at the peak of his fame after his April 1987 WrestleMania III match against Hulk Hogan at the Pontiac Silverdome — a match that drew 93,173 fans and ended with Hogan body-slamming the 520-pound Andre. The famous 'rhyming' scene where Fezzik recites poetry with Vizzini reportedly took multiple takes because Andre would lose his place. Reiner has said working with Andre was one of his life's great honors. The wrestler died January 27, 1993 in Paris.

question: Bryan Lee O'Malley's Scott Pilgrim graphic novels were originally published by Oni Press from 2004 to 2010 as small, black-and-white digest-sized paperbacks resembling Japanese manga. O'Malley drew the final volume's color art in part because the Netflix anime announcement had created industry curiosity.

question: The 2023 Mario Movie's Brooklyn opening uses a recreation of the original 1981 Donkey Kong arcade level as a literal training course. question: Released October 24, 1986, Don Bluth's An American Tail was the highest-grossing non-Disney animated film at the time, taking in $84 million on a $9M budget. The film was produced by Steven Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment and inspired by Spielberg's own Russian-Jewish heritage. The protagonist Fievel Mousekewitz was named after Spielberg's maternal grandfather. What was the grandfather's actual surname?
answer: Posner
context: Phillip 'Fievel' Posner emigrated from Ukraine to America in the early 20th century. The film's central song 'Somewhere Out There' (sung by Linda Ronstadt and James Ingram) was a top-5 hit. American Tail spawned a sequel (Fievel Goes West, 1991) and a TV series. Bluth left the franchise after the first film.

question: In 1985, when Steven Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment was assembling Back to the Future, the casting of Doc Brown went through several major changes. Christopher Lloyd was approached after the original choice rejected the role. The original choice had played Riff Raff in The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) and was a respected character actor at the time. Who was it?
answer: Jeff Goldblum was approached and declined, then Richard Donner suggested John Lithgow, who also declined
choices: Jeff Goldblum was approached and declined, then Richard Donner suggested John Lithgow, who also declined
Crispin Glover was originally offered Doc Brown before being recast as George McFly
Christopher Walken passed because he didn't understand the time-travel mechanics
Robin Williams demanded too much money and was passed over in favor of Lloyd
context: The original choice for Doc was actually neither Goldblum nor Lithgow — sources actually differ. Lloyd was offered the role and initially declined to spend time with his family. He took it after his wife encouraged him. Lloyd had played the Reverend in Taxi (1978-83) and was a Yale Drama School-trained character actor.

question: The original 1979 Don Bluth defection from Walt Disney Animation took 17 animators with him. Bluth had been at Disney since 1955 (working on Sleeping Beauty as a 17-year-old in-betweener) and was the lead animator on The Rescuers (1977). He left because of his frustration with what specific corporate trend at the studio?
answer: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail
choices: Disney was using xerography to cheapen the animation process and cutting fluid hand-drawn detail
Disney was outsourcing in-between animation work to a studio in Tokyo
Disney was about to license its characters to a kids' meal partnership at McDonald's
Disney was reorganizing its Burbank studio to share space with the theme parks
context: Bluth specifically named the loss of inking-by-hand and the elimination of multi-plane camera shots. Xerography (the photocopy-style process pioneered on 101 Dalmatians in 1961) gave a rougher line quality. Bluth's later films restored multi-plane and hand-inking. The Disney Renaissance starting with The Little Mermaid (1989) partly addressed his original grievances.

question: In 1983, Cinematronics released Don Bluth's Dragon's Lair as an arcade laserdisc game. The cabinet sold for $4,300 — roughly double a standard arcade cabinet's price. Players paid 50 cents per play (double the standard quarter). One year later, Sega Games released a Bluth follow-up using similar laserdisc technology with a space-opera theme. What was the 1984 follow-up called?
answer: Space Ace
context: Space Ace starred Dexter, the lasso-wielding space hero who transforms via the 'Infanto Ray.' Both Dragon's Lair and Space Ace ran on Pioneer LD-V1000 laserdisc players and used digital frame addressing for gameplay branching. American Laser Games later attempted live-action laserdisc games (Mad Dog McCree, 1990) that flopped.

question: Released June 25, 1982, Blade Runner had a famously troubled theatrical release. Test screenings in Denver and Dallas in May 1982 received hostile responses from audiences confused by the film's pacing and lack of narration. Warner Bros. forced Ridley Scott to add a Harrison Ford voiceover before the theatrical release. Ford reportedly delivered the voiceover badly on purpose, hoping it would be cut. What was added besides the voiceover?
answer: A 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining
choices: A 'happy ending' featuring outtake footage from Stanley Kubrick's The Shining
An opening expository newsreel explaining the off-world colonies
A new scene where Deckard explicitly states he's a replicant himself
A live-action prologue with Edward James Olmos's Gaff explaining the case
context: The aerial footage flying over forests was originally shot by Kubrick for The Shining's opening but unused. Scott borrowed the footage for the 1982 theatrical 'happy ending.' The 1992 Director's Cut and 2007 Final Cut removed both the voiceover and the happy ending, restored the unicorn dream sequence, and clarified Deckard's possible replicant identity.

question: Released in 1982, John Milius's Conan the Barbarian became Arnold Schwarzenegger's breakthrough role. Composer Basil Poledouris recorded the score in Italy with the Santa Cecilia Orchestra in Rome. Milius famously instructed Poledouris to create music 'as though Wagner had written it from the perspective of a Mongol horseman.' What instrument anchors the iconic 'Anvil of Crom' opening?

Solo cello over a string section playing the main theme in counterpoint
A brass-and-bone-flute fanfare over taiko drums
A Hungarian zither over a string ensemble in minor pentatonic
context: Poledouris hired blacksmiths to physically pound anvils on the studio floor for the percussion track. The choir sang in Latin (specifically: 'Doom upon all things, doom and woe' translated). The score became one of the most-licensed fantasy themes for film trailers in the next 40 years. Poledouris died in 2006 at age 61.

question: In 1993's Tombstone, Val Kilmer's Doc Holliday was widely considered the film's standout performance, eclipsing star Kurt Russell. Kilmer reportedly stayed in character with consumptive coughing for months. The film's original director was George P. Cosmatos, but Russell has long claimed he was the uncredited true director. The original director who was fired before filming began was the screenwriter himself. Who?
answer: Kevin Jarre, who also wrote Glory (1989) and the Tombstone screenplay itself
choices: Kevin Jarre, who also wrote Glory (1989) and the Tombstone screenplay itself
John Carpenter, who left over budget disputes with Disney's Hollywood Pictures
Andy Garcia, in his first attempted directorial debut after a delayed Godfather Part III
Steve Beck, the visual-effects supervisor who had directed second-unit work
context: Jarre was fired three weeks into shooting because the production was running behind. He had written a much longer epic screenplay; Cosmatos cut it considerably. Russell has said publicly that he 'ghost-directed' the film with Cosmatos as a paper-only credit. Jarre's screenplay credit remained intact. He died in 2011 at age 56.

question: Edgar Wright's 2010 Scott Pilgrim vs. the World was a financial disappointment on release ($47M on a $90M production+marketing budget) but became a cult favorite on home video. The film features Brandon Routh as Todd Ingram, Chris Evans as Lucas Lee, and Brie Larson as Envy Adams. Two of those cast members went on to play other comic-book heroes in the following decade. answer: Routh played Superman (Returns, 2006, pre-Scott Pilgrim) and Evans played Captain America (First Avenger, 2011)
choices: Routh played Superman (Returns, 2006, pre-Scott Pilgrim) and Evans played Captain America (First Avenger, 2011)

Evans played the Human Torch (Fantastic Four, 2005) and Routh played the Atom on CW
Larson played Squirrel Girl on a Marvel pilot and Evans played Captain America
context: All four answers are partially true. Routh played Superman in 2006 and the Atom on CW Arrowverse shows. Evans had played the Human Torch in 2005's Fantastic Four before becoming Cap in 2011. Larson played Captain Marvel starting in 2019. The Scott Pilgrim casting was prescient about which young actors would dominate the next decade.

question: Released in 1985, Steven Spielberg's The Goonies was directed by Richard Donner, who had earlier made The Omen (1976) and Superman (1978). The film's plot involves the kids finding the treasure map of a 17th-century pirate named One-Eyed Willy. What real-world pirate was Willy loosely based on?

One-Eyed Willy's ship 'The Inferno' was a full-scale practical-effect ship constructed for the climax — Donner refused to destroy it after filming, and crew members have said it sat in a warehouse for years.

question: Released in 1986, James Cameron's Aliens included the famous Colonial Marines led by Lieutenant Gorman. The Smartgun-wielding Vasquez (Jenette Goldstein) became an action-heroine icon. question: John McTiernan directed 1987's Predator. McTiernan had a remarkable run between 1987 and 1990, directing three iconic action films back-to-back-to-back. The other two films starred Bruce Willis and Sean Connery respectively. What were they?

question: Released in 1990, Paul Verhoeven's Total Recall featured one of the most expensive special-effects sequences in film history — the three-breasted Martian mutant prostitute scene. The actress who played the mutant Mary in the brief scene later became famous in television. Her name?
answer: Lycia Naff, who later played the Three-Breasted Whore (her IMDB credit) and went on to journalism

Naff later worked as an entertainment journalist for the National Enquirer.

question: In 1986, Tony Scott directed Top Gun on a $15M budget, which was high for a non-effects-driven film at the time. The Navy provided the F-14 Tomcats but required script approval. question: In 1986's Top Gun, the famous beach volleyball scene was added at the last minute by producer Don Simpson. The scene's homoerotic subtext has been widely discussed by film critics. question: In Princess Bride, William Goldman's 1973 novel famously frames itself as the abridgement of a fictional classic by 'S. Morgenstern.' question: Released in 1983, Don Bluth and Sega's Dragon's Lair laserdisc arcade game features Princess Daphne being held by the dragon Singe. question: Released in 1984, The Karate Kid was originally going to be set in Florida but was relocated to Los Angeles. Director John G. Avildsen had two specific reasons for the change. One was production logistics. What was the other?

question: In 1987's Predator, the original Predator costume was much more bug-like with a long neck. After Schwarzenegger and McTiernan saw the suit, they ordered a complete redesign. question: Released in 1990, the Italian-American Mafia subplot of Goodfellas was directed by Martin Scorsese. The film opens with Ray Liotta's iconic voiceover line. The screenplay was adapted from Nicholas Pileggi's 1985 nonfiction book. What was the book's original title?

question: Released in 1985, Robert Zemeckis's Back to the Future earned $381M worldwide on a $19M budget. The film famously features a Pepsi product placement in 1985 and 1955. What other beverage did Marty try to order in 1955 that wasn't yet available, becoming a famous gag?

question: Released in 1987, Mel Brooks's Spaceballs parodied Star Wars: A New Hope so closely that George Lucas reportedly approved the script personally. The film's parody character Lone Starr is paired with a beast sidekick named Barf, who's a 'mawg' — half-man, half-dog. Who played Barf?

question: John Williams's 1977 score for Star Wars: A New Hope was performed by the London Symphony Orchestra at Anvil Studios in Denham, England. question: Released in 1989, Don Bluth's All Dogs Go to Heaven famously released the same day as Disney's The Little Mermaid — November 17, 1989. The Disney film crushed it at the box office. question: Released in 1984, the original Karate Kid features Mr. Miyagi's wartime backstory — interned at Manzanar War Relocation Center during WWII while his wife and child died there. context: Morita was born in Isleton, California in 1932 to immigrant parents. He had spinal tuberculosis as a child and spent nine years in a Sacramento hospital. question: Released in 1985, Steven Spielberg's The Goonies was directed by Richard Donner. Donner had directed The Omen (1976) and Superman (1978). question: In 1986, Tony Scott's Top Gun was a financial massive ($357M worldwide on $15M budget). question: Released in 1989, the Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade Petra-temple sequence used the famous Al-Khazneh facade in Petra, Jordan. The interior temple was built on a UK soundstage. Steven Spielberg had previously used the Petra location for what other film concept that was never made?

question: Released in 1986, the Don Bluth/Steven Spielberg collaboration An American Tail was inspired by Spielberg's family history of Russian-Jewish immigration. The film's protagonist Fievel Mousekewitz was named after Spielberg's maternal grandfather Phillip 'Fievel' Posner. The film's iconic moment of Fievel briefly meeting Tanya in the steerage hold of the ship leaving Russia uses what specific 19th-century historical event as its backdrop?
answer: The Russian pogroms of the 1881-1884 period, which displaced over 2 million Eastern European Jews
choices: The Russian pogroms of the 1881-1884 period, which displaced over 2 million Eastern European Jews
The Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905, with Jewish refugees fleeing both conflicts

context: The American Tail era is specifically the 1880s-1890s Russian pogroms. Spielberg's grandfather Phillip Posner emigrated around this period. Fievel's separation from his family on the boat to America happens during a storm. The film's release in November 1986 was timed for the holiday season.
